extracted.intended_audience: learned Christians, theologians, and philosophers debating the possibility and nature of bodily resurrection
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical/theological argument showing the possibility of resurrection of the same proper body. The text distinguishes 'visible' and 'own' bodies, analyzes their components (fluids, solids, laws), and answers naturalistic and scriptural objections (children, missing limbs, emaciation, cannibalism) by appeal to experiments, metaphysical hypotheses, and analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use natural experiments to support possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observations and 'Chymical Experiments' that show how bodies and their parts can unite, be hindered, separated, or rejoined serve as sufficient evidence that a similar power could operate in the resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites chemical examples (salt of nitre uniting with steel unless an alkaline salt is present; salts mixing with oil to make soap undone by vinegar; iron and loadstone attracting or repelling) to show that everyday experiments suffice to show there is no impossibility in reuniting parts. The text emphasizes we need not accept specific naturalistic explanations — the truth of the experiments alone is enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: A bare hypothesis suffices to show possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove the possibility of a thing it is sufficient to produce an hypothesis that contains the manner in which it may come to pass and that includes no contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XIX: one need only 'find out an Hypotheſis containing the Manner how it may come to paſs, and which includes no Contradiction in it.' This standard is invoked to rebut atheistic demands for stronger demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish visible body from own (proper) body
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a visibly perceptible body ('visible body') and an individuating, proper body ('own body') which identifies the person even while many visible parts change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: saying a man 'weighs 200' refers to the visible body, while saying he 'is 80 years old' refers to the own body. The own body persists through changes of matter that compose the visible body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible body consists of three components: fluids, solids, and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The visible body is constituted of (1) various fluids (blood, chyle, glandular juices, etc.), (2) solid matter (flesh, bones, membranes), and (3) particular laws regulating digestion, separation of humours, nutrition, generation, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XXII enumerates fluids (blood, whey, lymph, milk, etc.), solid parts (flesh, bones, muscles, membranes, teeth), and the bodily laws that govern growth and change; these distinctions ground later claims about what is essential to identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluids are not essential to the own body
rubrics_metrics.description: Because bodily fluids are continually changed, separated, and replenished (daily loss of blood/humours, perspiration, effusions), they cannot be the essential constituents of the own body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XXIII argues by examples (large blood loss in women, continual change of humours) that the own body remains the same while fluids vary; therefore fluids are largely accidental to personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws (bodily functions) are not essential to the own body
rubrics_metrics.description: The particular laws that govern a living visible body (digestion, nutrition, motion) are changeable and cease at death, yet the own body can still be identified, so laws cannot constitute the essential own body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XXIII notes laws change with sickness, age, and cease when the body is dead, but the dead body is still reckoned the person's own body, showing laws are not essential constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Own body consists primarily of solid parts (chiefly bones and nerves)
rubrics_metrics.description: The own or proper body must be sought among the simple, enduring solid parts of the organism — especially bones and nerves (and membranes/tubes) — rather than fluids or mutable laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on the prior eliminations of fluids and laws (Sec. XXIII and XXXI), the author concludes the own body 'chiefly consist[s] of mere Bones' and the solid framework endures through changes and emaciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two conceptions of the own body: bare stamen or stamen plus accretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Either (a) the own body is a simple, primary principle or 'stamen' which unfolds and is later clothed with other matter, or (b) the own body includes that stamen together with accreted foreign particles that clad and fill it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XXIV sets up these two alternatives explicitly and uses them as separate bases for answering objections; in either conception the identity-preserving element is the stamen/seed principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resurrection condition if own body is a bare stamen
rubrics_metrics.description: If the own body is the bare stamen, resurrection requires that the stamen be preserved/continued and be unfolded, filled, and clothed (by the same or other matter) into a visible body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XXV explains that preserving the little substance (stamen) and allowing God to reclothe it with prior or new matter suffices for the same person to rise again; altered properties/faculties need not affect identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resurrection condition if own body includes accreted matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If the own body is the stamen plus some accreted matter, it still remains the same proper body despite continual replacement of much visible matter; resurrection can proceed by restoring or replacing the accreted parts in proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secs. XXVI–XXVIII use the ordinary fact that people acquire and lose vast quantities of matter over life (example: 1825 pounds of nutritive matter over 80 years) yet remain the same person to argue identity persists despite matter turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer to the 'child/imperfect body' objection
rubrics_metrics.description: A child who dies and is raised can be accounted the same person whether raised again as a child or as a full-grown adult because the stamen can be unfolded and filled to the relevant size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XXVIII: if the stamen remains and is later expanded and filled (as it would have been in life), the resulting body is the same proper body; analogy to natural growth is invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer to the 'missing limb' objection
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who lost a limb in youth would nevertheless rise with a full body because the relevant part of the stamen can be expanded, filled, and clothed in proportion at resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XXVIII: the same mechanism of expansion and reclothing of the stamen that explains childhood growth answers the missing-limb objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer to the 'emaciation' (wasted body) objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies much wasted by sickness may nevertheless be the same visible and own bodies; recovery shows that an emaciated visible body still contains the solid parts constitutive of identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sec. XXX and examples of persons reduced to skeleton-like leanness who later recovered show that visible bulk and fluid content vary without destroying identity; thus most persons who die emaciated can still rise with their own bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer to the 'cannibalism' objection
rubrics_metrics.description: That a cannibal ate many human bodies does not prevent each victim rising in his own body because nutritive processes separate the nourishing juices from the solid particles (the 'stamina' or own-body principle), which may remain distinct or be restored at resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secs. XXIX–XXXIII argue that what nourishes the eater is the fluids/gravy, not the solid own-body particles; solids and the stamen are not necessarily converted into the eater's own stamen and thus may appear separate and entire at resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural hermeneutic: leave manner to God and reconcile passages by appeal to power and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not insist on a human account of the exact manner of resurrection; apparent scriptural tensions (e.g., Paul's grain-of-seed analogy vs. texts claiming the same body) are resolved by noting that God may change the manner as pleases Him and by appealing to natural analogies and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secs. XVII–XVIII: the author warns that the manner is a 'great Mystery' to be left to God; reconciliation proceeds by noting that an hypothesis showing no contradiction plus empirical analogies is sufficient, and by interpreting scripture in light of God's power and the facts of experience.
